entries.title: Proverbs 9:1
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Her house - For the reception of her guests. Seven - Many pillars; whereby is intimated the beauty and stability of the church. Pillars - Prophets, and apostles, and ministers.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:2
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Killed - Made provision for the guests. Mingled - With water, as they used to do in those hot countries. Furnished - With all necessaries, and now waits for the guests.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:3
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Maidens - Her servants to invite the guests, ministers of the word whom he calls maidens for the decency of the parable; for wisdom being compared to a great princess, was fit to be attended upon by maidens. Highest places - From such high seats as those from which judges delivered their sentences, and officers made proclamations.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:7
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: A former - He shews whom he meant by the foolish, ver. 6 , even scorners and wicked men, and presses his last advice of forsaking them because there was no good, but hurt to be got from them.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:8
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: A scorner - An obstinate and incorrigible sinner.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:12
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: For thyself - Thou dost not profit me but thyself.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:14
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: At the door - Watching for occasions of sin.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:15
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Go right - Who are going innocently about their business.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:16
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Simple - This title is not given them by her, but by Solomon.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:17
entries.author: John Wesley (1703–1791)
entries.content: Sweet - From the difficulty of obtaining them; and because the very prohibition renders them more grateful to corrupt nature.
